articles.title_orig: COP31 Talks Collapse in Turkey in a Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.title_zh: COP31 Talks Collapse in Turkey in a Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.content_orig:
EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey .
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.
The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”
Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.
But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”
Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”

Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”
Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.
The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.
But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.
While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño , the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.
“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

articles.title_zh: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire at the port early on Sunday morning
An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.

Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.

articles.title_orig: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels
articles.title_zh: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels
articles.content_orig:
COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.
The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions .
After the EU walked out, so did other countries pushing for a speedy transition away from fossil fuels.
The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Negotiations at this year's U.N. Climate Summit were supposed to end Friday but there was no agreement on language about fossil fuels. Activists demonstrated by holding signs that read "shame" at COP31, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow, of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."
NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits .

articles.title_zh: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship set ablaze in Baltic Sea drifts into Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship set ablaze in Baltic Sea drifts into Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
Rescue and firefighting efforts are continuing for a Russian cargo vessel hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, authorities have said.
The ship - the Sparta II - was bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday that work was ongoing to make sure the cargo ship did not sink but it was not aware of any danger to surrounding maritime traffic.
Water was still being used to douse the ship on Sunday, and Finland said Estonian and Russian assets were also involved in recovery work.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used in the strike, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

A Russian drone strike partially destroyed a five-story apartment building near Kyiv, leaving 14 people unaccounted for, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
Rescuers were searching the rubble in Dymer, north of Kyiv, where part of the building collapsed and a fire broke out. Nine people had been evacuated, Zelenskyy added, warning that others could remain trapped.
The attack prompted the Ukrainian president to renew pressure on Washington to approve deliveries of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles financed by Ukraine’s allies, amid mounting Russian aerial attacks. “It is particularly difficult to understand the delays in supplying anti-ballistic interceptors to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said on X .
He urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles already paid for by Ukraine’s partners through NATO’s PURL program , which allows allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said earlier this month that deliveries under the program, including Patriots, were continuing.
Russia launched 186 drones overnight, including 72 jet-powered models, Ukraine’s air force said. Ukrainian defenses shot down or disabled 161, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked 20 Ukrainian regions over the past week, launching around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles.
Many were ballistic missiles, including North Korean-made weapons, he said, accusing Moscow of helping Pyongyang improve their accuracy.

articles.content_orig:
If there's anything we could add to GTA 6 as things stand, it'd be an official 60FPS mode. That's obviously not possible right now due to how demanding the game is on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S hardware, even in the case of the PS5 Pro.
Interestingly though, over the weekend, players have discovered the ability to activate what some are calling a "60FPS Glitch" or "60FPS Bug" on Xbox consoles, forcing the game to unlock its FPS and run at a higher frame rate than it's actually supposed to.
Someone called Meowwie64 on Reddit appears to have found this, and here's what they did to activate it:
Now, as mentioned, there are multiple drawbacks here. The first one is that the glitch speeds up most aspects of the game, making it run faster than intended (and look like it's in fast-forward mode!). This is obviously not an ideal way to enjoy GTA 6, and serves as an immediate deal-breaker in my view.
Another one is that reaching 60FPS is pretty much impossible under normal gameplay circumstances. If you're driving down a highway, for example, you're likely only going to get around 35-40FPS at max, with 60FPS and above being saved for situations that require no graphical intensity whatsoever.
And finally, it should be noted that GTA 6 was never intended to be run this way on Xbox Series X|S, and therefore you could run into all sorts of issues - crashes, bugs, maybe even your console overheating. That last one is unlikely, but the game has been specifically built to run at 30FPS on these machines, so it's not worth pushing it in our view.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Although the AI industry has been the darling of Wall Street for years, the sector now makes investors wince as it reckons with a wave of concerns over dizzying spending and its promise to make the technology profitable.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index was indicative of this shift after plummeting 5.28 percent on Friday, wiping out all gains it had recorded since the start of the year.
"Markets were euphoric" about AI but "there's a huge repricing going on right now," Steve Sostick, a financial analyst with Interactive Brokers, told AFP.
The so-called "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks largely driving the market -- Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta and Tesla -- have seen their combined market capitalization fall by more than $4 trillion in the past month-and-a-half, according to an AFP analysis based on Bloomberg data -- a decrease larger than the annual GDP of France.
"You have a situation now where the bubble already deflated...The question now is how far down will it go?" Adam Sarhan, head of the financial platform MarketTerminal.com, told AFP in an interview.
- US midterms and Nvidia controversy -
While the trajectory of stock markets is never linear, the setbacks have piled up on tech darlings this month.
First, US midterm elections dominated by Democrats "really turned the tide, as it told us that American voters are not fans of artificial intelligence," Sostick said, referencing the many local ballot box measures restricting data centers.
Second, the biggest company in the semiconductor industry, Nvidia, has seen its longtime chief Jensen Huang resign over multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funneled restricted chips to that country.
With the chip market being so key to the AI industry, the disruption has had widespread ripple effects in the stock market.
"The AI investment boom has gone from a promising technology story to a capital markets extravaganza," said Stephen Innes, a manager at SPI Asset Management, with billions of dollars spent to develop the technology.
But as spending has ballooned, so has debt -- and profits have yet to match.
"As the capital needs grew, we started to see investors question how profitable all these investments might be, whether all this money was being spent wisely...the market hadn't been really asking these questions before," Sostick said.
"It seems absurd to ask people to invest money and not have a real sense of what's going to be the return on that investment," he added.
AI giant Anthropic, maker of Claude AI software, made its stock market debut Thursday, raking in an eye-watering $91 billion.
However, even with such a windfall, the company has acknowledged that its financing needs could require it to borrow money in the future.
"The opaqueness of AI-related debt is further compounded by circular links in the form of mutual commitments and interlinked ownerships between firms in the AI supply chain," the European Central Bank warned in a recent report.

ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Delays are mounting across the country for Delta Air Lines flights after a ground stop and ground delay caused by a technical issue, the Atlanta-based airline said.
A ground stop issued Sunday morning for Delta flights on their way to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport turned into a ground delay, the FAA said Sunday.
The ground delay, which is in effect until at least 1 p.m., means that flights on the ground heading to Atlanta will now be allowed to depart, but they are being delayed nearly an hour.
The ground delays are due to a problem with Delta’s weight and balance automation system, the Atlanta-based airline said.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said.
Because flights are taking longer to depart due to Delta personnel having to manually calculate their weight, it is limiting gate space for arriving flights, exacerbating the delays.
“We are working with our air traffic control counterparts to strategically enact programs to protect airport gates and tarmac areas from congestion at our Atlanta hub,” Delta said.
Delta passengers are reporting delays at multiple US airports online, including Atlanta, Newark, LaGuardia, Reagan National, Dulles, Boston, Baltimore, Miami, Minneapolis, Nashville, San Antonio, Birmingham.
Just before 10 a.m., nearly 500 flights were delayed at the airport, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking website.
The delays come just as the busy Thanksgiving travel period is about to begin. Officials at Hartsfield-Jackson airport expect more than 4 million passengers through Dec. 1, up 5% from last year.

articles.title_orig: Correction or deeper reckoning? Investors seek signs US stock selling will abate
articles.title_zh: Correction or deeper reckoning? Investors seek signs US stock selling will abate
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 lost 8.6% this week and closed 6% below its 200-day average. Earnings haven’t cracked, which makes this a liquidity event. The question is whether the Fed blinks before the break hardens.
Last week, in VIX Spike: Complacency’s Bill Coming Due , we warned that low volatility eventually begets high volatility. That bill came due early. The S&P 500 fell 8.6% to 6,910, its seventh straight losing session and the longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq-100 dropped 10.4%, the Dow lost 8.0%, and the Russell 2000 slid 7.5%. At 11.6% below its October 6 record, the index is in “correction” territory, and the VIX nearly doubled to 37.
So was this a liquidation of leveraged positions due to margin calls? Partly, but not the way the headlines suggest. FINRA’s latest data put margin debt at $1.45 trillion in October, down 2.1% from September and 3.6% below June’s record. Margin borrowing was already easing before the week began.
What we saw instead was mechanical deleveraging. On Thursday, just 38 S&P 500 stocks rose while 464 fell, and all 11 sectors finished lower, even staples. Goldman’s Rich Privorotsky called it “a pretty violent liquidation” in a note covered by ZeroHedge. Dealers were heavily short gamma into Friday’s monthly options expiration, which fed the afternoon selling. Desk chatter also had investors selling gold, copper, crypto and Nvidia to fund allocations in Anthropic’s IPO , which priced at $83 on Wednesday. Gold fell 9.5%, copper 10.2% and Bitcoin broke below $60,000.
Macro supplied the trigger. Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a 50-basis-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting after a third straight 0.3% monthly gain in core CPI. The Commerce Department’s rule restricting remote access to advanced AI chips by Chinese firms took effect on Thursday, landing on the AI supply chain the same day. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.91% from 5.15%. The bond market is starting to price a growth problem, while the Fed is still fighting an inflation problem.
Here is the real question that needs an answer. “Have the fundamentals changed?” Not yet. Through FactSet’s November 13 update, analysts had raised fourth-quarter EPS estimates 1.1% since September 30, something that rarely happens mid-quarter, and third-quarter earnings grew 31.9%.
The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow still tracks fourth-quarter growth at 3.4%, and initial jobless claims of 203,000 remain near historic lows. Cracks are showing only at the edges. The Philadelphia Fed index collapsed to 6.3 against expectations of 20, the Conference Board’s leading index fell 0.3%, and existing home sales hit their slowest pace since 2010. So far, this is a valuation and liquidity event, not an earnings recession. At 6,910, the S&P 500 trades near 16.6 times FactSet’s November 5 forward earnings estimate of $415.82, down from 17.7 times on that date.
This suggests that the liquidation of positions is likely “overdone.” Since 1950, the S&P 500 has suffered 17 separate episodes in which it fell 8% or more over five sessions. It was higher three months later in 15 of them, with a median gain of 8.1% . The catch is that the median further drawdown along the way was 4.5%, so the bottom rarely arrives on schedule.
Next week, the main focus will be on the Federal Reserve. If Wednesday’s PCE data cools and Fed speakers soften, the setup for a reflexive rally is in place. If not, Privorotsky’s 2018 comparison, when the Fed kept hiking and stocks didn’t bottom until Christmas Eve , becomes the playbook .
The S&P 500 closed Friday, November 20, at 6,910.39, down 8.6% for the week. That leaves the index 6.0% below its 200-day average at 7,348.58 and 9.4% below its 50-day average at 7,625.25. It closed below the lower 2-standard-deviation Bollinger Band at 7,094. It also finished just 18 points above the lower 3-SD band at 6,892. To wit: the index ended the week 2.9 standard deviations below its 20-day mean.
The technical backdrop is telling a more interesting story. First, momentum is confirming the extreme selling pressure this past week. On Friday, the 14-day RSI fell to 24.7. That is its lowest reading since April 8, 2025. That date is important as it marked the bottom of the tariff-driven selloff. Notably, during that selloff, the market was being priced for an impact on earnings growth from tariffs. However, currently, analysts continue to maintain or raise earnings estimates for the fourth quarter and next year.
Secondly, the MACD sits at −130 index points, well below its signal line at −75, and Williams %R is at −97. Such is what a forced-selling week looks like on a chart. Oversold is a condition, not a buy signal, and it can persist longer than anyone expects during a liquidation.
Third, breadth tells a more nuanced story. The equal-weight S&P 500 fell 6.1% against 8.4% for the cap-weighted S&P 500 index. The damage has been largely concentrated in the AI complex, with Technology falling 12.3%. However,  semiconductors (SMH) dropped 17.8%, while Nvidia lost 22.9%.
Even the more defensive sectors couldn’t avoid the selling pressure. Staples and Utilities lost 2.0% and 3.0%, respectively. In other words, defensive stocks did their job of reducing the volatility, but they didn’t avoid it. The average stock is in better shape than the index, which helps any rebound broaden. But leadership is what broke, and leadership rarely heals in a week.
Volatility and bonds tell you what kind of selloff this is. The VIX closed at 37.24, nearly double last Friday’s 19.30. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell 24 basis points, and the long-bond ETF (TLT) gained 2.6% while nearly everything else fell. When bonds rally as stocks drop, investors are running from risk rather than scrambling for cash. Watch that relationship next week. If Treasuries start selling off alongside stocks, the liquidation has moved into a more dangerous phase.
In our portfolios, we used the decline to nibble on NVDA and PANW this week. However, these were very small additions, and something that we will likely continue to do into further weakness. Notably, these are NOT calls that the market has bottomed. Next week, we’ll trim value positions to raise cash. That keeps the dip buys from adding to overall equity exposure while the index sits below a level that matters this much. Our 7,000 risk line gave way on Friday, and we’re treating it that way.
For more aggressive traders, the playbook is to let the rubber band snap before acting. With the market at a 2.9-standard deviation (SD) extreme, a reflexive rally toward the lower 2-SD band near 7,094 should be expected. That is a tradeable reflex rally, but should be treated as a strict trade with defined exits.
The 200-day average at 7,349 is the first real test above the market currently. For now, use any rallies into that zone to rebalance and reduce risk rather than chase. However, on the downside, the 3-SD band at 6,892 is only a thin level of support. Any decisive break opens the April 7 close of 6,617, where the spring rally launched.
Next week, there is only one market level that really matters: 7,349. Any snapback toward the 200-day average would be normal from an oversold extreme this deep. What matters is whether the index can close and hold above it. That action will decide whether this break joins the healed ones or the deep breaks that keep going.
This coming week, Thanksgiving will compress everything into just three trading sessions. Markets are closed on Thursday, and then the market will close early at 1:00 p.m. ET on Friday. For investors, this is a week to turn off monitors and enjoy your family, as the thin holiday trading tends to magnify moves in both directions. With the VIX sitting at 37, this is where investors tend to make mistakes.

articles.title_orig: A Physicist Built a Black Hole on a Chip. Then It Started to Leak.
articles.title_zh: A Physicist Built a Black Hole on a Chip. Then It Started to Leak.
articles.content_orig:
Black holes do many things.
They sit in space, slurping up matter, drawing spacetime around them like a cozy blanket, and firing off powerful jets of near-light-speed plasma.
What they are not especially good at is letting go.
But when physicist Antonino Flachi of Keio University in Japan built an analog black hole on a chip, something strange happened at its tiny event horizon – something that, in a real black hole, would be forbidden by the laws of general relativity.
When he poked a hole – metaphorically speaking – the black hole began to leak.
It's an experiment that offers physicists a new tool for probing which properties of black holes are universal – and which might change when the rules of physics do.
"Digital circuits thus form a reconfigurable class of gravitational analogs," Flachi writes in a preprint (yet to undergo peer review) uploaded to arXiv , "and realize an analog black hole as a cellular automaton."
Their penchant for absorbing light and letting nothing detectable escape from within their event horizons means they're invisible to most of the tools we use for studying the cosmos – telescopes that rely on the electromagnetic spectrum.
However, the mathematics describing the behavior of black holes can be used to build laboratory experiments that replicate some of their properties and behaviors so that we can study what they are capable of .
One way to do this is with sound.
Sound waves traveling through a moving fluid can behave in ways very similar to light traveling through the curved spacetime around a black hole. If the fluid flows inward faster than sound can travel outward, the sound waves become trapped, unable to escape the current.
This creates what physicists call an acoustic black hole.
But what if you could build an acoustic black hole without all the mess and fuss of speakers, fluids, and currents?
This is what Flachi has done, replacing the entire kit and kaboodle with a compact digital circuit.
"We have built an analog black hole out of logic gates," he writes .
"Its horizon is a property not of the wiring but of the state: a closed curve in a lattice of 32-bit words along which the emergent flow carries disturbances inward exactly as fast as they spread outward."
He calls his system a 'digital acoustic black hole', a circuit that contains a grid of cells, each storing information as a series of bits – the ones and zeros that form the basis of digital computing. The grid stored a total of around 604 million bits.
At each tick of a clock, logic gates update the information in each cell according to a set of rules based on fluid dynamics, creating the digital equivalent of water flowing inward toward a drain.
These rules also govern how disturbances travel through the grid. Where the simulated flow carries those disturbances inward as fast as they can travel outward, an acoustic event horizon emerges.
Unlike a physical fluid, which can be unpredictable and difficult to control, the precisely defined rules for the digital acoustic black hole make the digital fluid far more controllable. Experiments can even be repeated under identical conditions, right down to the individual bits.
To test his creation, Flachi measured five properties of the simulated black hole: the stability of its event horizon, the horizon itself, the way disturbances propagate through it, its response to being disturbed (the ringdown), and a phenomenon called superradiance, in which waves can gain energy from a rotating black hole.
It performed brilliantly. The event horizon remained stable for 3 hours, and the circuit demonstrated ringdown and superradiance, consistent with the mathematical predictions.
But then, Flachi got curious. He wanted to know what would happen if he changed one small thing.
Inside the event horizon, he flipped just one of the system's 604 million bits – and it was as though the black hole had sprung a leak.
Flipping the bit created an acoustic disturbance in the black hole. Most of it remained contained beyond the event horizon – as you would expect for something taking place behind that boundary.
But a small fraction of the disturbance escaped, carried by short-wavelength waves that could travel faster than the effective speed of sound in the circuit.
So the event horizon worked as expected for longer waves, but was not quite so impenetrable to shorter ones.
And the deeper inside the horizon Flachi flipped the bit, the less of the disturbance escaped. The leakage diminished exponentially with distance from the boundary.
This doesn't mean that real black holes have leaky event horizons – but it reveals something important about black hole analogs. The behavior of their horizons isn't necessarily universal, but can depend on the underlying physics of the system in which they emerge.
And Flachi's system offers a new way to poke them. He has shown that a functioning black hole analog can be built entirely out of digital logic – one whose underlying rules are precisely known and finely controllable.
This means that it can be used to probe the physics of black hole horizons, and to explore new scenarios that reveal what might be possible if the rules of physics were bent just a teeny tiny iota.
The paper has not yet been peer-reviewed, but a preprint is available on arXiv .

articles.title_orig: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes
articles.title_zh: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes
articles.content_orig:
Hackers are stepping up attacks on U.S. ports and cargo ships, targeting computer systems that keep goods and energy exports moving.
The attacks have intensified in recent months, with breaches reported at ports, aboard oil tankers, and at a major shipping company, Financial Times reported on Sunday.
The chief executive of the nation's largest crude oil export hub, the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas, says his port faces hundreds or even thousands of attempted intrusions each day.
At Corpus Christi, which handles about 2.3 million barrels of crude oil exports a day, hackers have probed networks and sent messages impersonating senior executives to trick employees into granting access.
"They're poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities," Port of Corpus Christi CEO Kent Britton said. "With AI, it'll only get more complicated."
Corpus Christi is preparing to hire its fourth cybersecurity staff member and is seeking additional help from Washington.
If an attack takes its systems offline, tugboats can escort vessels through parts of the channel, and the harbor master's office can use two-way radios, binoculars, and paper records to keep traffic moving.
Britton said some of the attempts came from states and organizations known for malicious activity. He declined to identify them.
The FBI recently warned that hackers are using artificial intelligence to automate attacks.
The U.S. Coast Guard said increasingly connected computer networks and equipment controls mean a breach can shut a terminal gate, interrupt cargo handling, or disrupt ship systems, putting crews and supply chains at risk.
An Aug. 4 cyberattack disrupted operations at all three North Carolina Ports facilities, in Wilmington, Morehead City, and Charlotte, WECT in Wilmington, North Carolina, reported.
The agency activated its cybersecurity contingency plan and brought in state and federal partners, including the Coast Guard.
"In Wilmington, the operations team implemented a delayed opening and transitioned to manual gate processing, allowing the IT team to focus on system recovery efforts," a North Carolina Ports spokesperson told the station.
The agency contained the breach and began restoring its systems.
At the time of WECT's report, officials had yet to identify who was responsible or give a timeline for full restoration.
The spokesperson said there was no indication sensitive data had been compromised.
The Coast Guard reported a 17% increase in maritime cyber incidents last year.
In August, the agency and the FBI boarded two foreign-flagged tankers after indications their networks had been compromised near the Strait of Gibraltar.
The vessels were carrying crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas from the Mediterranean to Galveston, Texas.
Investigators have yet to publicly identify suspects.
The Port of Los Angeles said it blocked 120 million attempted attacks in August, including automated attempts, nearly double its monthly average in 2023.
Shipping company Maersk said hackers stole data in a breach this month and that its operations continued without disruption.
The Coast Guard issued maritime cybersecurity rules in 2025 requiring covered operators to report qualifying cyber incidents to the National Response Center and provide annual training to personnel with access to computer networks or equipment controls.
The rules cover U.S.-flagged vessels and maritime facilities, including facilities on the Outer Continental Shelf, that already must maintain Coast Guard-approved security plans.
By July 16, 2027, covered owners and operators must designate a cybersecurity officer, complete an assessment, and submit a cybersecurity plan to the Coast Guard for approval.
"Early preparation is absolutely critical," said Rear Adm. Robert Compher, the Coast Guard's assistant commandant for prevention policy.
The agency said it also checks for cyber risks during inspections of foreign-flagged ships.
In serious cases, it can detain a vessel, deny it entry or restrict its movement until the risk is addressed.
The Port of Virginia conducts monthly employee training and holds drills with the Coast Guard. Port spokesperson Joe Harris said it had yet to suffer a successful breach.
"We're an economic pinch point," Harris said. "Getting taken offline is not an option."

articles.title_zh: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.content_orig:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain, as Iran has intensified attacks over the past week, hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and downing US drones.
At least 25 tankers have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, in the past seven days, causing the Gulf oil flow to drop sharply.
The escalating attacks come as Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country is facing what he called a “silent economic war” amid US sanctions and a naval blockade.
So what is behind Iran’s latest escalation, and will it trigger a new round of hostilities between Tehran and Washington or force the two sides to sit down for talks to end the war that has caused a global energy crisis?
Bahrain has faced the brunt of Iran’s attacks in recent days.
On Saturday, Manama said an Iranian strike hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire , as it thwarted several other attacks that day.
The IRGC said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, claiming to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
Iranian state media reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain crashed on Sitra Island near Manama, sparking a large fire.
The IRGC said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Iran has justified the attacks as a response to continued violations of its airspace, including by US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones.
Bahrain has faced three drone attacks in recent days after a lull in fighting for several weeks.
Iran’s army on Saturday said its air defences fired a missile at a US F-16 jet over the Gulf the previous evening, damaging the aircraft, the IRNA news agency reported. However, US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, stating that “all US fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for”.
Iranian forces on Sunday also said they shot down another MQ-1 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC claimed it was the 20th US drone of this type to be shot down since the war began in late February and the fourth in the past 24 hours.
Meanwhile, British maritime authorities reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman.
Al Jazeera correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week, with about 25 since November 14.
Last week, the Iranian army also said it targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base. The attack came after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under effective Iranian control.
Oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz has seen a considerable dip as Iran has escalated attacks on a near-daily basis.
According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), 263 ships passed through the key waterway between November 12 and 18, which is 15 percent fewer than the previous week and 20 percent fewer than the week before that.
Of those vessels, 37 were oil tankers, down from 52 the previous week, UKMTO reported on Friday.
The figures, however, could be higher as vessels passing through as part of shadow fleets are not officially registered.
About 135 ships passed daily through the vital strait before the war began in February.
Last week, the US maritime agency warned that the Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums, with insurance rates up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war to 3.5-7.5 percent.
Oil prices have spiked, crossing $100 a barrel before settling down to $83, still more than $15 from before the war.
Cumulative losses from the conflict have now reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
The IEA, however, added that the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4 percent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response.
As Iran has ramped up attacks, senior officials have asked the US to choose between surrendering to missiles or to diplomacy.
The attacks indicate that Iran is using its leverage in the conflict, sending the message that the US allies in the region will continue to bear the brunt of its actions if the war does not end.
The attacks aim to diminish US military capabilities in the region and “also to spread the pain of the war widely to include the entire [Gulf region] and, indirectly, global economies via higher shipping costs and stressed supplies of essentials”, Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, told Al Jazeera.
The single biggest driver of this strategy, Khouri said, is for Iran to continually ensure that it will no longer “suffer alone from US-Israel-imperial assaults”.
Tehran is hoping to change US policy by revealing its inability to protect its own facilities or those of its Arab allies, which could prompt Arab governments to press US President Donald Trump to end the war, Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, added.
Meanwhile, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that he considers the economic blockade imposed by the US on Iran an act of war.
“We consider the economic siege a hostile act, and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” Gharibabadi told Iranian reporters.
The ongoing US naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and a wave of new sanctions imposed in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast are hurting Iran economically.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran, has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027.
However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure.
The strikes on US interests in the Gulf in recent days have therefore been viewed as a defiant response to the US campaign. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.
Trump may choose to declare victory and walk away from the war on Iran rather than negotiate a deal, but continuing the naval blockade on Iran would risk further military escalation, says Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Parsi said Trump was unlikely to accept an agreement that could be seen in Washington as showing the war had failed.
“If he continues the blockade, there will be escalation,” Parsi warned, arguing that Iran would not refrain from retaliating against continued economic pressure.
He said Trump would need to “slowly, perhaps imperceptibly, lift the blockade, as well as lift some of the sanctions” if he wanted to withdraw from the confrontation without renewed fighting.
Hassan Ahmadian, professor at the University of Tehran, said Iran is forcing a “binary” choice on Trump.
If Washington lets the tankers pass, the US blockade “ends without an agreement or war”, Ahmadian said on X. However, if the US attacks the vessels, it could face “Iranian responses that will be difficult for [Trump] to avoid”.
Trump said on Saturday he had plans to make a deal with Iran that is “permanent” and prevents it from getting a nuclear weapon.
He also told US broadcaster Fox News that he was never very interested in regime change in Iran, but called its new leadership “more rational”.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”

articles.title_zh: From Anthropic to Nvidia, Wall Street just had a bizarre, wild week
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
I have seen a lot in the investing world over the past 20 years. Mostly good. A lot of bad.
But I have to say: This past week will live on with me until I retire.
Anthropic ( ANT ) just put a $1.2 trillion price tag on the AI dream. The AI lab opened its first trading day on Thursday at $111.50 per share — well above its $83 per share IPO price — and closed out Friday at $88. The company has dethroned Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) as the largest IPO in history, raising $81 billion in its IPO compared to $75 billion for SpaceX.
The stock opened for trading on the Nasdaq around 11:45 a.m. ET — earlier than many thought it would — under the ticker symbol ANT. (Ants are also what Anthropic's employees call one another — true story.)
Speaking of the Nasdaq, things were pretty much locked down over there. We weren't allowed in the booth to record or go live. It's my understanding that's how Anthropic wanted it, or at least this was the prepared line.
I find it bizarre that a company trying to hype its do-gooder vibes kept media out of the building. An array of reputable media outlets broadcast from the Nasdaq each day. To keep them out on the directive of Silicon Valley elites and their PR handlers is surprising.
Tens of millions of average investors were studying Anthropic on IPO day, and this company pretty much said, "Go read the S-1 and leave us alone."
I can tell you a lot of good people were not happy about this, including a few inside the frontier AI lab. But maybe at this point in the year, nothing should surprise me!
Meanwhile, over at Nvidia, the mood is a whole lot darker .
The company that made this AI boom possible continues to face a stunning leadership crisis even as it tried to make a clean break from founder Jensen Huang on its earnings day this past week. Jensen Huang is gone. Employees are rattled.
At the first company-wide all-hands meeting without Huang on late Wednesday, interim CEO Colette Kress basically played corporate therapist by promising raises, promising more stock, and trying to keep people from walking out the door.
Oddly though, Kress didn't take any employee questions directly. I find this bizarre too, and so have others, judging by the messages I received on X. An all-hands meeting is supposed to be for employees to ask questions of leadership, not just for leadership to talk to employees.
Nonetheless, Anthropic cashed in on AI mania, while Nvidia is trying to hold its workforce together. Interesting times in investing!

A fire on board a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones off the coast of Finland in the Baltic Sea continued to burn through the night even as efforts were made to douse the flames, the Finnish coastguard said.
Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remains at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.
Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.
The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

Later ⁠on Sunday, one person was ⁠killed when a Russian drone struck a grocery store in Vyshneve, southwest of Kyiv, the local governor said on Telegram, adding that three ⁠people were injured.

articles.title_orig: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.title_zh: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.content_orig:
Pain, swelling, and stiffness in the knees can be downright debilitating.
As cartilage breaks down in these joints, it can significantly reduce freedom of movement and cause pain, even when standing still or sitting.
Surprisingly enough, core exercises may be a neglected form of treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
A randomized controlled trial in India has now found that working out the abdominal muscles may have a trickle-down effect for the knees.
Strengthening the abdomen won't stop cartilage from degenerating, but in this particular trial, when core exercises were added to typical rehabilitation programs, it improved physical function more than conventional exercises alone.
What's more, patients who did the core exercises also reported significantly less pain when moving about.
The findings are published in Scientific Reports , and while the study is small, the methodology was rigorously designed.
The trial involved 100 participants, aged 40 to 80, with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis.
Roughly half the group were randomized to partake in conventional knee-focused rehabilitation for 12 weeks.
During the trial, this half of the group partook in 45 minutes of supervised exercise three times a week for four weeks.
Each session involved progressive strengthening, range-of-motion, and functional exercises, such as straight-leg raises and moves to strengthen the quadriceps.
Participants then continued these exercises at home on their own for an additional 8 weeks.
Meanwhile, the other half of the group was randomized to undertake a different rehabilitation program.
This one involved a mix of conventional knee-based rehabilitation exercises and progressive core-targeting exercises.
The core exercises included abdominal bracing, glute bridges, forearm planks, arm raises while lying down, heel taps, and alternating arm-and-leg movements similar to dead bugs.
After the 12-week intervention period, both groups demonstrated significant reductions in resting pain.
But it was the group that also partook in core training that demonstrated greater improvements in physical function tests and reported less pain when moving about.
Importantly, this group also reported greater improvements in their quality of life.
The authors of the study don't know why core training led to these benefits, but they suggest that an improvement in posture control may help stabilize the body's core during exercise, putting less strain on the lower limbs.
"Collectively," the team concludes , "these biomechanical adaptations provide a plausible explanation for the greater improvement observed in pain, physical function, and quality of life compared with conventional knee-focused strengthening alone."
The findings are supported by previous research, which also suggests that the core is a neglected part of knee pain.
In 2021, for instance, a peer-reviewed narrative review argued that despite preliminary findings that core training is beneficial for knee issues, more research is needed.
"Investigations that show it is safe and effective in older adults have not been adapted to/incorporated into treatment recommendations for those with knee osteoarthritis," the authors argued.
This year, the results of several randomized clinical trials have begun to roll in.
One trial among 48 patients with knee osteoarthritis in Pakistan, for example, also found that adding core stability training to knee exercises produced greater improvements in pain, knee mobility, and quality of life after 12 weeks.
Plus, a larger study of 100 patients found that adding core exercises to conventional knee rehabilitation was more effective than adding foot-and-ankle strengthening.
That seemed to be particularly true for outcomes like pain and physical function.
Related: Study of 33,500 CT Scans Challenges a Common Assumption About Ab Strength And Back Pain
These randomized trials are small, but their findings suggest that exclusively targeting the joints during osteoarthritis treatment may not be the best move.
The whole body is connected, and the function of our extremities is founded upon the stability of our trunk.
Ab exercises may help cut to the core of the issue.
The research has been published in Scientific Reports .
